title: The dead philosophers
hookLine: Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Socrates: all gone, and all did their work (Meditations 6.47)

cards: The stones in an old cemetery read like a town meeting: a doctor, a schoolteacher, a child, a soldier, somebody's beloved grandmother. Each one was the center of a whole world, and now the names are fading in the rain.
It can feel crushing. Or it can feel like company. Marcus Aurelius took that walk in his head, in book six, and the stones he read had some very well-known names on them.

teach.h: EVERY KIND OF PERSON HAS DIED.
teach.b: In Meditations six, forty-seven, Marcus tells himself to keep in mind that people of every kind, every trade and every nation have died. Then he names them. Great speakers.
Noble philosophers: Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Socrates. Heroes of old days, generals and tyrants. Then the sharp minds: Eudoxus, Hipparchus, Archimedes, men of keen natural talent, as he puts it.
All in the dust, he says, where we're all going. These aren't strangers to him; he names Heraclitus and Socrates elsewhere in the Meditations too. Remembering that even they died doesn't shrink them.
It puts him in their line. If Socrates had to die, Marcus can stop acting as if he won't.
Then the turn: what's left that's worth a great deal? To live through life in truth and justice, and to be kindly even toward liars and the unjust.
The dead philosophers didn't escape death.
They did their work, and in Marcus's sense that's the part that lasts: it was done. Every one of us is downstream of someone who taught us and is gone. A grandparent who explained how to be honest.

A teacher who saw something in you. A writer you read once at nineteen. Remembering them on purpose is a practice Marcus kept: book one of the Meditations is Marcus thanking, one by one, the people who formed him.

how: Some readers of Marcus keep a habit like his book one: naming and thanking the teachers, living and dead, who formed them, and remembering that the great ones also died after doing their work.

a sharp mind Marcus names among the dead, all in the dust

games.q: the dead philosophers — tap the pairs.
p: Marcus thanks those who formed him

s: Marcus lists Heraclitus, Pythagoras and Socrates among the dead
6.47 names them among the noble philosophers who have gone.
Marcus uses the list to say their work meant nothing
he turns to what's worth much: living in truth and justice, kind even to the unjust.

games.q: you're reading a long list of great people who have all died. what does Marcus say is worth a great deal?
o: becoming well-known enough to be on the list.
living in truth and justice, kindly even toward the unjust.
games.why: Meditations 6.47 ends: one thing here is worth much, to live in truth and justice, with kindness even toward liars and the unjust.

practice: Bring to mind one teacher of yours who has died, a relative, a mentor, an author, and recall one thing they taught you, in words or by example. Say their name quietly and thank them in whatever way is natural for you.
Then rest in the plain fact that some of their work is in you now.

wordCard.voice: Archimedes, one of the sharp minds Marcus names among the dead, all in the dust where we're all going, and what remained was their work. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: philosopher; 6.47 names Heraclitus, Pythagoras and Socrates among the philosophers.

carryVoice: Your line: they did their work. Truth and justice, lived while there's time, are what's worth much. That's day five hundred eighty-three.
